Why firm accountsWhy the talk asks how sanctions worked, and not whether

How sanctions worked shows in firm accounts, whatever the sender sought.

Whether sanctions work depends on what the sender wanted. How they worked at the level of the firm can be measured under any of those aims.

In the dissertation: Introduction
OpeningSettingFrameworkDataChapter 2Chapter 3What follows4 / 85

A3 · Opening

Whether sanctions work is the question the literature has asked most often and answered least well, because what counts as success depends on whether the sender sought deterrence, concessions, or damage.

Firm accounts show how firms adjusted under any of these aims. I use them to ask two questions about firms that bear on import substitution versus scarring.

An economy can appear resilient partly because of which firms remain observable. To study how firms adjusted, we first need to know whose accounts we can see.

The debateThe debate the research question is about

Import substitution predicts that domestic firms expand most where firms with foreign or joint ownership lose most.

Galbraith reads sanctions on a large market economy as quotas or tariff walls. If so, the slope across industries is near one. The register records each firm’s ownership.

In the dissertation: Introduction, Section 1.2.3.1
OpeningSettingFrameworkDataChapter 2Chapter 3What follows5 / 85

A4 · Opening

The register records whether a firm was foreign-owned or jointly owned in that year. This group includes Russian businesses held through foreign companies.

James Galbraith argues that, so long as internal demand is maintained, in a large market economy like that of Russia effective sanctions operate like quotas or tariff walls. He compares them to trade protection combined with a robust industrial policy. On that reading sanctions invite import substitution. Sonnenfeld and coauthors argue the opposite in the title of their paper, that business retreats and sanctions are crippling the Russian economy.

The two readings differ on one observable. If domestic firms replace what firms with foreign or joint ownership lose, then across industries the gain at other firms rises with the loss, along the dashed line. If they do not, the points lie flat. Chapter 3 estimates that slope across 572 four-digit industries, and the talk returns to this picture with the estimate drawn in.

Scarring in the full sense is a loss that outlasts the restriction. We need accounts from after the restriction ends to establish it.

I’ll return to this picture twice. In Chapter 3 I’ll show the regression and the industries it compares. In the last part I’ll add the estimated slope to this picture.

The research questionThe question, in the dissertation’s words

How do financial visibility and adjustment differ across Russian firms under sanctions, how are these differences related to firms’ resources, and what do they imply for import substitution versus scarring?

Chapter 2 asks which firms stay visible in the public accounts. Chapter 3 asks how the firms that stay visible adjusted.

In the dissertation: Introduction, Table 2.1, Table B.1
OpeningSettingFrameworkDataChapter 2Chapter 3What follows6 / 85

A5 · Opening

I break the dissertation’s research question into two questions about firms.

Chapter 2 asks which firms’ statements remain publicly available, and how availability relates to a firm’s size and financial position. Chapter 3 asks whether firms with more cash or inventories sustained sales and operating margins, and whether privately owned firms gained where firms with foreign or joint ownership had held more of an industry’s sales.

Consider the firms we can follow from 2021. Of 3,357,109 eligible firms, 2,129,509 had an available statement, and 1,503,173 enter the cash sample that Chapter 3 follows. Whose accounts we can see determines whose adjustment we can study.

The next slide defines the terms this one uses.

TermsThe working vocabulary of the data

What these terms mean throughout the talk.

In the dissertation: Table A.4, Section 2.2.1, Section 2.2.2
OpeningSettingFrameworkDataChapter 2Chapter 3What follows7 / 85

A6 · Opening

These terms have the same meaning throughout the dissertation. Table A.4 defines each measure, population, sample, and group and points to the section that explains it.

“Eligible” is the RFSD’s classification. The RFSD starts from the register of legal entities and removes organizations the law exempts from filing an unconsolidated statement. It excludes government bodies, state-owned public service providers, religious organizations, financial firms that report to the Bank of Russia, and firms incorporated in the last quarter of the year. The remaining firms count as eligible whether or not a statement is available. A firm the RFSD marks as eligible may still have a legal exemption or a restriction on public access to its statements. Keeping firms without statements in the population lets Chapter 2 measure visibility.

A statement counts as available when the release marks it as filed and not imputed. A filed statement with flagged amounts still counts. I exclude its amounts from every financial measure.

Removal comes from the dated registry record and takes precedence over a statement filed for the year of dissolution.

I hold membership in the five lists fixed across years. Membership alone tells us neither when a firm was designated nor whether it had a legal entitlement or used disclosure protection.

The last entry defines the two interpretations in the research question. The next slide gives the findings, and the last part returns to those interpretations.

The answerThe answer first, in three findings

The accounts through 2024 give three findings.

Which firms can be observed is selective. By 2024 the gap for firms on the sanctions list was 12.6 points. Full replacement is rejected at the 5% level.

In the dissertation: Figure 2.1, Section 2.6.2, Figure 3.5
OpeningSettingFrameworkDataChapter 2Chapter 3What follows8 / 85

A7 · Opening

Each key press shows one of the three findings and the numbers behind it.

First, public statements did not become scarcer under sanctions. The share of eligible firms with an available statement rose from 63.4% in 2021 to 66.3% in 2024, as firms without statements left the register. The firms whose statements stay public are the larger and financially stronger ones.

Second, firms on the sanctions list alone were more visible than comparable firms on no list in 2013 to 2018. In 2021 their predicted probability of an available statement was 1.1 percentage points lower than that of comparable firms on no list. By 2024 it was 12.6 points lower.

Third, recorded sales at firms with foreign or joint ownership fell by 34.7% between 2021 and 2024. Across 572 four-digit industries a larger loss predicted no additional gain at other firms. The replacement slope, the gain at other firms for each ruble lost, is −0.23 with a 95% confidence interval from −0.64 to +0.18, so full replacement, a slope of one, is rejected at the 5% level.

To explain these three findings, I’ll start with why firms might want to withhold their accounts. The framework describes the two decisions firms face, and the two empirical chapters test the predictions. I’ll return to all three findings at the close.

Part one

Setting

How sanctions came to work through banks and firms, and how Russia prepared.

Terms in this part

Designation
One listing of a target on one sanctions list. A target on several lists has several records.
Smart sanctions
Measures aimed at the elite supporters of a regime and designed to impose minimal hardship on the wider public.
Weaponized interdependence
A state with authority over the central hubs of a network through which money, goods, and information travel can use that position to coerce others. Cutting an adversary off from the network’s flows is the chokepoint effect. The term is Farrell and Newman’s.
Overcompliance
Private banks and firms going beyond the strict legal requirements of a sanction. The term is Newman and Zhang’s.
Correspondent relationship
An account relationship that links banks across countries and currencies and lets them send and receive cross-border payments.

B0 · Setting

These twelve slides cover the institutional background in Chapter 1. They explain why firms had reason to withhold their public accounts.

The five terms come from several sources. The dissertation counts designations as defined in Table A.2. For smart sanctions I follow Drezner, for weaponized interdependence Farrell and Newman, for overcompliance Newman and Zhang, and for correspondent relationships Matvos and Neiman.

1914 to 2022How sanctions came to aim at banks and firms

A century took sanctions from blockading populations to targeting banks.

Wilson called the economic weapon a “peaceful, silent, deadly remedy.” Smart sanctions were later designed to spare the wider population.

In the dissertation: Section 1.1.1
OpeningSettingFrameworkDataChapter 2Chapter 3What follows10 / 85

B1 · Setting

In the First World War the Entente blockaded the Central Powers. Wartime disease and malnutrition resulted in an estimated 480,000 to 800,000 civilian deaths. Woodrow Wilson presented the boycott as an economic, peaceful, silent, deadly remedy that would leave no need for force (quoted in Mulder, The Economic Weapon).

In 1990 UN Security Council Resolution 661 banned imports of all commodities and products originating in Iraq or Kuwait. The toll of that embargo is disputed and is counted in the hundreds of thousands. Drezner describes what followed as smart sanctions, the precision-guided munitions of economic statecraft, designed to hurt elite supporters of the targeted regime while imposing minimal hardship on the mass public.

From 2006 the US Treasury turned to banks. In 2014 the same architecture was extended to Russia, and in 2022 it reached the central bank’s reserves.

The rest of this part traces how sanctions extended from banks in 2006 to central bank reserves in 2022. That history explains why Russian firms had reason to withhold their public accounts.

Iran · 2006 to 2010How private banks became the enforcers

Stuart Levey turned banks’ commercial incentives into enforcement.

Levey set out in 2006 to enlist the world’s banks. By his account, private actors often went beyond the strict legal requirements.

In the dissertation: Section 1.1.2
OpeningSettingFrameworkDataChapter 2Chapter 3What follows11 / 85

B2 · Setting

Stuart Levey was the Treasury’s Under Secretary for Terrorism and Financial Intelligence. In January 2006 he read that a large Swiss bank had cut off business with Tehran, and decided to mobilize the private sector, starting with the world’s banks (Wright, New York Times Magazine, 2008).

The diagram follows his testimony to the House Committee on Foreign Affairs of 1 December 2010. Designations raise the commercial risk of doing business with Iran. The 2010 sanctions act then forces what he calls a stark choice between that business and access to the US financial system. As more banks and firms cut off their dealings, the reputational risk increases for those that have not, which he describes as a mutually-reinforcing cycle of governmental and private sector action. Newman and Zhang call the result overcompliance.

Treasury Secretary Henry Paulson denied that anyone was threatened. Foreign bankers told the reporter that the threat was always implicit.

I’ll return to this episode twice. The framework expresses Levey’s stark choice as a condition for compliance. The opacity index in Chapter 2 draws on the cost to Iran when counterparties could no longer distinguish legitimate from illicit transactions. Those counterparties cut off Iran entirely. Concealment can let some transactions through and still cost a firm business with its counterparties.

Iran · June to December 2010Evasion met by enforcement, route by route

“Whenever we find a loophole, they block it.”

An Iranian official, September 2010. Since June the Treasury had updated the entries of 71 blocked vessels and exposed 53 front companies of one shipping line.

In the dissertation: Section 1.1.2
OpeningSettingFrameworkDataChapter 2Chapter 3What follows12 / 85

B3 · Setting

Levey designed the program to be, in his words, specifically adaptive and responsive to Iranian evasion attempts. Iranian banks stripped their names from transaction documents. Banks that were not designated stepped into the shoes of those that were. The state shipping line IRISL renamed and repainted its ships and changed their nominal ownership.

The Treasury responded by updating individual entries. Since June 2010 it had designated 53 front companies of the shipping line and 9 of its officials, identified 27 more vessels as blocked property, and updated the entries of 71 vessels already blocked to give their new names.

The quotation is from a high-ranking Iranian official in September 2010, as Levey reports it to Congress. Enforcement and evasion adapt to each other.

Evasion · 2017 to 2023Evasion as an industry that outlasts one target

“Iran’s ghost fleet now carries Russian oil.”

Russian oil on dark ships, tankers that switch off their transceivers, surged after the embargoes and price caps of late 2022.

In the dissertation: Section 1.1.2
OpeningSettingFrameworkDataChapter 2Chapter 3What follows13 / 85

B4 · Setting

The sentence is Jesús Fernández-Villaverde’s, from his remarks at the 2026 Jackson Hole symposium. It closes a longer point. Evasion is an industry with fixed costs. Build the capacity once and it serves the next target.

The figure is his Figure 7, from his paper with Li, Xu, and Zanetti on tankers that switch off their identification signals. The stacked bars show how much crude these tankers carried from four sanctioned countries each month. Shipments from Russia rose from the end of 2022.

The dissertation takes one point from the episode. Concealment keeps some trade moving, and the capacity built to evade one sanctions regime serves the next target.

Russia · 2021 to 2025The chokepoint in practice

Russian banks’ cross-border correspondent relationships fell from 1,050 to 242.

Sanctioned Russian banks rose from 41 to 100. What remained rerouted toward yuan clearing through Chinese banks and tenge clearing through Kazakhstan.

In the dissertation: Section 1.1.4
OpeningSettingFrameworkDataChapter 2Chapter 3What follows14 / 85

B5 · Setting

The opening slide of this part defined the chokepoint effect as cutting an adversary off from a network’s flows. Here we can see how many connections Russian banks lost.

Matvos and Neiman map the correspondent accounts through which banks reach foreign currencies. Between September 2021 and November 2025 the number of Russian financial institutions under US, EU, or UK designation rose from 41 to 100, and the cross-border correspondent relationships of Russian banks fell from 1,050 to 242.

The figure is theirs. Each band is a group of relationships by currency and country. Dollar, euro, and pound relationships nearly disappear, and yuan and tenge relationships remain.

Matvos and Neiman measure the remaining access in two ways. For the country as a whole, one surviving link to a hub is enough, so the loss of centrality is small. When they measure access bank by bank and aggregate across banks, the loss is much larger. Most Russian banks lost access to the key hubs even though at least one kept it.

2022The same instruments, turned on Russia in 2022

February to June 2022. The reserves frozen, the ruble at 120, the coupons unpaid.

The default was recorded as Russia’s first external default in a century. Breydo calls it a political default, imposed despite having the money.

In the dissertation: Section 1.1.3
OpeningSettingFrameworkDataChapter 2Chapter 3What follows15 / 85

B6 · Setting

Four months, read from left to right.

In late February the G7 immobilized more than $300 billion of the central bank’s foreign reserves. Lipsky calls it the single most important geoeconomic decision of the decade so far. The central bank suspended stock trading on the Moscow Exchange from 28 February to 21 March.

By mid-March the ruble had fallen from about 75 to 120 per dollar, and depositors had withdrawn a record 1.3 trillion rubles within days. The central bank raised its rate at the end of February and imposed capital controls. Nabiullina’s rule for the episode is that speed takes precedence over precision.

On 31 March a decree required buyers in countries Russia calls unfriendly to pay for pipeline gas through ruble accounts at Gazprombank, and on 27 April Gazprom halted deliveries to Bulgaria and Poland.

The US license that let bondholders receive Russia’s payments expired on 25 May. In late June about $100 million in coupons, which Russia had already remitted, failed to reach bondholders through the blocked clearing chain.

The next slide stays on the first of these events.

February 2022 · The reservesWeaponized interdependence, at the scale of a central bank

More than $300 billion in Russian central bank assets was immobilized. Lipsky writes that allies could now jointly weaponize payment systems at a moment’s notice.

In the dissertation: Section 1.1.3
OpeningSettingFrameworkDataChapter 2Chapter 3What follows16 / 85

B6a · Setting

Lipsky describes the reserve freeze, the first event on the last slide. He chairs international economics at the Atlantic Council in Washington and founded its GeoEconomics Center. The two sentences come from different paragraphs of the same article.

The freeze shows how weaponized interdependence can reach a central bank. On the earlier slides about banks and a shipping line, a private firm had to choose between doing business with a target and keeping access to the dollar system. In February 2022 the coalition used its position in that same network against the reserves of a G20 state.

Lipsky’s reading is that Russia’s diversification into euros after 2014, which he calls a rational approach at the time, no longer worked once allies acted jointly.

The next slides show the limits of the freeze. The central bank had been preparing since 2014. The framework in the next part explains how that preparation matters.

June 2022A default made by closing the channel for payment

The 2022 default came from closed payment channels, with the money already remitted.

Breydo calls it a political default, imposed “despite having the money, and seemingly wanting to pay.”

In the dissertation: Section 1.1.3
OpeningSettingFrameworkDataChapter 2Chapter 3What follows17 / 85

B7 · Setting

Washington at first licensed the receipt of payments on Russian bonds. That safe harbour expired on 25 May 2022. Russia had settled its April arrears with dollars from outside the frozen reserves and prepaid coupons ahead of the expiry.

In late June about $100 million in coupons, funds Russia had already remitted, failed to reach bondholders through the blocked clearing chain. The episode was recorded as Russia’s first external default in a century, over the finance minister’s objection that it was in no way a default.

Russia had the resources to pay. By closing the channel those payments would have used, the sender exposed Russia to a contrived default.

The Bank of Russia · 2014 to 2022How the target prepared after 2014

Elvira Nabiullina sought to fortify the financial system against exclusion.

“Speed takes precedence over precision.” The 2022 response drew on credibility built after 2014.

In the dissertation: Section 1.1.3
OpeningSettingFrameworkDataChapter 2Chapter 3What follows18 / 85

B8 · Setting

Russia had already taken steps that mattered when the freeze came. The framework in the next part explains how that preparation affects the sender’s power.

After 2014 the Bank of Russia diversified its reserves across currencies and locations, which Nabiullina describes as a guard against both economic and geopolitical risks, and it brought inflation down between 2015 and 2019. The manuscript also records the domestic Mir card system, developed from 2014.

When the 2022 measures arrived, the ruble fell from about 75 to 120 per dollar by mid-March and depositors withdrew a record 1.3 trillion rubles within days. The Bank raised its rate at the end of February and introduced capital account measures in March, most of which it lifted by mid-year. In her account the market remembered the 2014 rate rise and understood that high rates could bring inflation down.

She had opposed capital controls before 2022. She reconsidered when sanctions themselves, in her words, served as a form of external capital controls.

Settlement · 2025 to 2026Overcompliance again, on a route built to avoid the dollar

Alternative settlement still depends on willing counterparties.

The ruble stablecoin A7A5 lost 96% of its daily volume within a year of its peak, as exchanges froze or flagged funds that had touched it.

In the dissertation: Section 1.1.4
OpeningSettingFrameworkDataChapter 2Chapter 3What follows19 / 85

B9 · Setting

On the slide about Levey, banks went beyond what the law required. Here we see exchanges do the same for a token designed to bypass banks.

A7A5 is a ruble token issued from Kyrgyzstan and backed, according to its operators, by deposits at a sanctioned Russian state bank. It offered a route into dollar-pegged stablecoins outside conventional banking channels.

Sanctions targeted its issuer and the exchanges tied to it. The token kept operating, and other exchanges used transaction screening to flag or freeze deposits linked to it. In June 2026 its transaction volume averaged $24.3 million a day, down 96% from its July 2025 peak. Elliptic also records restrictions on Russian retail access and the failure of the token’s main trading venue, so the decline does not purely isolate the effect of Western sanctions.

The same limit applies to conventional channels. By 2023, 53% of currency trading already took place over the counter through the banking system, and on 12 June 2024 the US Treasury designated the Moscow Exchange and its clearing and depository institutions.

A separate ledger is not sufficient for independent payment access. Convertibility still depends on counterparties willing and able to process the transaction.

Leakage · 2022 to 2023Rerouting, which the framework counts as leakage

Two rerouting channels offset about one third of the sanctioned decline in European exports.

Goods reached Russia through Armenia, Kazakhstan, and Kyrgyzstan, or were declared for those countries and stopped in Russia.

In the dissertation: Section 1.2.3.1, Introduction
OpeningSettingFrameworkDataChapter 2Chapter 3What follows20 / 85

B10 · Setting

Chupilkin and coauthors use product-level export data to identify goods under EU sanctions. They document two channels. The first is trade intermediated through countries outside the sanctions regime. The second is the misreporting of destinations, where goods nominally shipped to neighboring countries via Russia fail to reach their declared destination.

For Armenia, Kazakhstan, and the Kyrgyz Republic, the two channels together offset roughly one third of the decline in direct European exports to Russia prompted by product-specific sanctions over 2022 to 2023.

The Introduction gives a second example from the same period, a 1,860% increase in UK vehicle exports to Azerbaijan.

Trade through third countries illustrates leakage in the framework that follows. A threat gives the sender less power when there is a chance it will never be carried out.

Disclosure rules · 2020 to 2023The rule that makes withholding accounts lawful

From 2022 a firm could ask the tax service to close its accounts to public view.

The list of firms authorized not to disclose began with 11 names and passed 1,000 after 2022. Chapter 2 measures which firms then stay visible.

In the dissertation: Section 2.2.1
OpeningSettingFrameworkDataChapter 2Chapter 3What follows21 / 85

B12 · Setting

Two rules allowed firms to keep their accounts out of public view.

Under Government Decree No. 35 of January 2020, major firms were authorized not to disclose their financial statements. The RFSD’s authors report that the list initially included 11 firms and was expanded after 2022 to cover more than 1,000. They count 1,133 firms on the list of strategic companies by the end of 2023.

Under the special procedure of 2022, an organization providing its 2021 accounts could apply to the Federal Tax Service for full restriction of public access. Full restriction covered all years beginning in 2019, without a choice of individual years. From 1 January 2023, Decree No. 1624 carried those restrictions forward. Access restriction did not remove filing duties.

The article counts the lists as issued. The estimates use the smaller groups matched to the register. There are 22 eligible firms on the 2020 filing-exemption list. The group on the government’s strategic list alone includes 426 firms in 2021.

An absent public statement can reflect a firm’s choice to withhold its accounts. The next part models that choice. This rule gives firms the entitlement to withhold that appears in the model.

Part two

Framework

Geoeconomic power, and two decisions a firm makes under it.

Terms in this part

Participation constraint
The condition under which a target complies with a sender’s demand. Complying must be worth at least as much to it as refusing.
Leakage
The chance that a threat is not carried out, as when a sanction is evaded. It lowers the sender’s power.
Opacity
A firm’s accounts are absent from public view. Its measured counterpart is the absence of an available statement.
Substitution capacity
The share of its loss from a restriction that a firm recovers once it has paid the sunk cost of reorganizing.
OpeningSettingFrameworkDataChapter 2Chapter 3What follows22 / 85

C0 · Framework

I start with Clayton, Maggiori, and Schreger’s model of geoeconomic power and add two decisions firms face in the target economy. One is whether to keep their accounts public. The other is whether to reorganize production or trade.

Geoeconomic power · Clayton, Maggiori, and SchregerLevey’s stark choice, written as a condition

A target complies while complying is worth at least as much as refusing. The gap is the sender’s power.

The sender widens the gap by degrading the outside option or improving the inside one. Evasion narrows it. A threat carried out only some of the time makes refusing worth more.

In the dissertation: Section 1.3.2.1, Section 1.3.2.3, Figure 1.1
OpeningSettingFrameworkDataChapter 2Chapter 3What follows23 / 85

C1 · Framework

On the earlier slide, Levey described a stark choice. A bank that does certain business with Iran risks losing access to the US financial system. Here we can write down the condition under which it complies.

In Clayton, Maggiori, and Schreger’s framework, the sender, which they call the hegemon, wants a target to take an action. It offers a favorable environment if the target complies and threatens an unfavorable one if it refuses. The target complies when doing so pays at least as much as its best option under the threat.

The example in smaller type is the authors’ own. The United States might ask a German bank to reduce its business with Iran. If the bank complies, its American subsidiaries may continue to access the Federal Reserve’s emergency lending facilities. If it refuses, it may face full exclusion from the dollar-based financial system.

The sender’s power is the gap between the target’s value in the two environments. That gap is the most the sender can ask the target to give up.

On the second key press, leakage. If a threat is carried out only with probability pi, the value of refusing is a mixture of the two environments, and the room for a demand shrinks. Evasion reduces power. Trade rerouted through third countries is leakage in this sense.

The authors assume that the foreign government is passive when its firms face coercion, an assumption they call not innocuous. The Russian state supports its firms and changes their options. I’ll return to that role on the slide about the domestic constraint.

Geoeconomic power · Clayton, Maggiori, and SchregerWhere the banks and payment systems of the setting fit

Micro-Power is what one target will bear. Macro-Power is what that is worth to the sender.

A target weighs only its private cost. The sender collects the value across the system. The authors’ examples of strategic sectors include payments and finance.

In the dissertation: Section 1.2.1.2, Equation 1.1
OpeningSettingFrameworkDataChapter 2Chapter 3What follows24 / 85

C1a · Framework

The last slide showed one target’s choice. The equation at the top distinguishes two questions for the sender. What can it demand, and what is compliance worth to it? The sender chooses the demand that maximizes its own welfare, subject to the target being willing to comply.

Micro-Power sits in the constraint. The authors define it as the maximal private cost to the entity of the actions the hegemon can demand. The dissertation’s example is a European bank pressed to cut off Iranian clients. It weighs only its forgone business. The short stroke across a link in the drawing marks a relationship that has been severed.

On the second key press, Macro-Power. The authors define it as the social value to the hegemon of the costly actions it demands of the targeted entities. The sender values the cumulative squeeze on Iran’s economy that many such severed relationships jointly produce. The bank does not count that value, and the sender does. The sender exploits the difference between the private cost to the target and the social benefit to itself.

Recall the slides on Levey and on correspondent banking. The authors give dollar-based payment and clearing systems as an example of a strategic asset in the micro sense. They also name finance as a candidate for a strategic sector in the macro sense. Micro-Power is most valuable when the sender holds it over sectors that generate Macro-Power.

The authors explicitly link Micro-Power to the participation constraint. This slide interprets Macro-Power as the value the sender’s objective in Equation 1.1 places on its demand. Neither the authors nor the dissertation states that second link in a single sentence.

Geoeconomic power · The price of a threatWhat makes the gap on the last two slides large or small

A cutoff costs a target more the larger the share it loses and the harder that share is to replace.

The loss has a closed form. Near monopoly, the last points of control are worth the most.

In the dissertation: Section 1.3.2.2, Equation 1.2
OpeningSettingFrameworkDataChapter 2Chapter 3What follows25 / 85

C1b · Framework

The last two slides described the sender’s power in terms of a gap between two values. How large can that gap be when the threat is a ban on sales to the target?

Clayton, Maggiori, and Schreger give the loss in closed form. It rises with the share of the target’s spending that falls on the threatened goods, and it is larger the harder those goods are to substitute. In their production structure the inputs are substitutes when the elasticity is above one, and the formula is for that case. They show that the same forces drive a threat to cut off capital.

The curve on the right shows the loss at a fixed elasticity. As the controlled share approaches one, the loss rises without bound. Near monopoly, a small decline in the share costs the sender much of its power.

The next slide is the authors’ estimate of how much of that power the coalition had lost over Russia before 2022.

Preparation · 2005 to 2021How much of that power was gone before 2022

The coalition’s share fell from 94% to 84%, and its financial power over Russia approximately halved.

Power is convex in the controlled share, so a sender that loses a little control near monopoly loses much of its power.

In the dissertation: Section 1.3.2.3
OpeningSettingFrameworkDataChapter 2Chapter 3What follows26 / 85

C2 · Framework

The formula on the last slide says power is convex in the controlled share. This is the authors’ estimate of what that meant for Russia.

Clayton, Maggiori, and Schreger estimate that the share of Russian financial imports controlled by the American coalition was a stable 94% before 2014 and dropped to 84% as Russia reduced its financial dependence. They estimate that the coalition’s financial power over Russia was approximately halved by 2021 compared with 2014, and they attribute part of the muted effect of the financial sanctions imposed after 2022 to that loss.

In the authors’ figure, one line shows the coalition’s share of Russian financial imports. The other shows their measure of its financial power over Russia.

The mechanism is convexity. In the cutoff-loss formula the loss from a threat grows without bound as the controlled share approaches one, so diversification before 2022 could reduce the loss from a later cutoff by much more than the change in the share suggests.

The target state’s sideWhy pressure on elites can bind them to the state

He gives these among the reasons sanctions work worst against entrenched autocracies. The next slide writes the regime’s side as a constraint.

C2a · Framework

So far we’ve considered the sender’s decisions. The authors’ model of coercing foreign firms assumes a passive foreign government. The Russian government takes an active role.

Fernández-Villaverde lists reasons sanctions work worst against entrenched autocracies. The two passages on this slide give his first two reasons and appear one after the other in his handout. The other two are that firms find work-arounds and networks reroute. Recall the tankers and the trade through third countries in the earlier slides.

The second sentence is the one the dissertation builds on. If the regime decides who collects the rents, then a firm’s standing with its own state becomes part of what a sanction changes.

The domestic constraintThe same constraint, held by the target state over its own firms

Sanctions meant to turn elites against the state can deepen their dependence on it.

An owner stays loyal while the value inside the bargain is at least the value of exit. Designation is assumed to cut the value of exit by more.

In the dissertation: Section 1.3.3, Equation 1.4, Figure 1.1

C2b · Framework

This is the participation constraint of three slides ago with the roles changed. The party making the offer is the target government, and the party choosing is a politically connected owner.

Before 2014 the owner’s outside option was strong. Russian business elites held foreign wealth as a hedge against their own state, and a survivable exit limited what could be demanded of them. Personal designation freezes what an owner holds in coalition jurisdictions. What survives of the owner’s earning capacity concentrates in firms that operate at the state’s discretion.

The dissertation compares the owner’s options. The value of staying rises with state support and with the entitlement to withhold accounts. The alternative is to exit. The state can make a costly demand as long as staying is worth at least as much to the owner as leaving.

On the second key press, consider what designation by the sender does to those options. The model assumes designation reduces the value of exit more than the value of staying. The state can then demand more of the owner. State support also lets it demand more, at a cost to the state.

Two pieces of outside evidence point the same way. McDowell and Steinberg find that the share of Russians who favor saving in foreign currency fell from 18.7% in three surveys before the 2022 sanctions to 7.8% in five surveys after. Surveys of savers do not measure oligarchs’ offshore holdings.

The RFSD records legal entities and their accounts. The owner’s options and the state’s demands are unobserved. The empirical chapters can test patterns among firms, including what the opacity index predicts for firms entitled to withhold.

The opacity index · Chapter 2The first of two decisions a firm makes under this pressure

A firm withholds its accounts when protection is worth more than the business it would lose.

Hiding the accounts also hides the firm from its own lenders, suppliers, and customers. Each quantity has a prediction and a measure that stands in for it.

In the dissertation: Section 2.3, Equation 2.1, Equation 2.2Try it in the web edition

C3 · Framework

The framework explains how a sender puts pressure on a firm. I add two decisions the firm faces under that pressure. The first is whether to keep its accounts public.

Start with why a firm would hide. Public statements can inform the compliance checks that banks and other intermediaries run, so a visible firm is easier to press. Withholding the accounts shields the firm from that. The benefit rises with enforcement pressure.

Why, then, do most firms keep their accounts public? Consider a firm applying for a loan or bidding for a supply contract. A bank, supplier, or customer that cannot verify the firm may decline to do business with it, even if both parties are domestic. The more business the firm has at stake with its counterparties, the more costly it is to withhold. The cost is lower for a firm entitled to withhold.

The firm withholds when the net return is positive. An unobserved component turns the rule into a probability, and with a logistic distribution it is the logit that Chapter 2 estimates.

On the second key press, the three predictions and what stands in for each. The registry records none of the three quantities. Membership of the sanctions list stands in for pressure, the 2020 filing-exemption list for the entitlement, and total assets for the business at stake, on the assumption that a larger firm has more business with customers, suppliers, and lenders who require public accounts. Chapter 2 takes these three rows one at a time, and its last slide sets the three results side by side.

The model is static. It predicts which firms are opaque in a given year and leaves open when they become so.

The web edition has this figure with controls for the three quantities.

The adaptation boundary · Chapter 3The second decision a firm makes, whether to reorganize

A firm reorganizes when the profit it expects to recover covers the sunk cost.

A longer expected restriction lowers the boundary, and a higher sunk cost raises it. The accounts record two resources that bear on the decision.

In the dissertation: Section 3.3, Equation 3.2, Figure 3.1Move the boundary in the web edition
OpeningSettingFrameworkDataChapter 2Chapter 3What follows30 / 85

C4 · Framework

The opacity index described the first decision a firm faces under pressure, whether to keep its accounts public. The second is whether to reorganize.

The adaptation model has two periods and follows the tradition of Dixit and Baldwin. A restriction binds in the first period and may persist into the second. A firm exposed to restricted inputs loses profit in each period the restriction binds. Paying a sunk cost lets it recover part of that loss. A firm with greater substitution capacity recovers more.

The boundary is the level of substitution capacity at which the discounted gain from adapting equals the sunk cost. A firm adapts if and only if its capacity reaches that level or exceeds it. Multiplying the discount factor by the probability the restriction persists gives the effective discount factor. A higher effective discount factor lowers the boundary. A higher sunk cost raises it. When part of the cost is fixed, the boundary falls as exposure rises. At sufficiently low exposure, no firm adapts.

On the second key press, what Chapter 3 takes from the model. The RFSD does not record exposure or capacity, so the boundary itself is not estimated. The accounts do record two resources that bear on the decision. Cash is a means of paying the sunk cost, so its gain should show in the second and third years. Inventories sustain sales while a firm seeks another supplier, so their advantage should come first. Chapter 3 puts each resource under its prediction.

The model leaves out the option value of waiting that the cited dynamic models contain.

The web edition has this figure with sliders for its three parameters.

The Russian Financial Statements DatabaseThe data that make both questions answerable

The RFSD holds 63.3 million firm-year records for 2011* to 2025*.

It is the first open database of financial statements covering Russia’s eligible firm population, including firms whose statements are unavailable.

In the dissertation: Section 1.4.1, Table B.1 · * No filed statements for 2011. 2025 is on revised forms and is an extension (Sections 1.4.4, 2.2.1).

D1 · Data

The RFSD was built by Bondarkov, Ledenev, and Skougarevskiy. Their article describes it as the first open data set with information on every active firm in the country, including non-filing firms. The release used here is version 3.1.0, with 63,308,662 annual records.

The registry includes firms whose accounts we cannot see. In 2021, 3,357,109 firms were eligible and 2,129,509 had an available statement. Keeping all eligible firms lets us study which ones remain visible.

The eligible population has fallen every year since 2016, while the number of statements has stayed between 2.0 and 2.2 million since 2015. That pattern returns in Chapter 2.

The approach · Chapter 2What lets the question of who stays visible be asked at all

The register keeps a firm in the data when its statement is missing, so absence becomes an outcome.

A database of statements cannot tell a firm that stopped filing from one that closed. Chapter 2 measures availability for every eligible firm and sets it against exit.

The left panel shows what we’d see in a database of filed statements. Firms B and C both disappear after 2021. From those records alone we cannot tell why. Firm E never appears, and firms D and F both appear for the first time partway through.

On the right is what the RFSD holds for the same six firms. It starts from the register of legal entities, so an eligible firm has a record whether or not it filed. On the second key press, what Chapter 2 does with this. The outcome is whether a statement is available, for every eligible firm in every year, 20.6 million firm-years from 2019 to 2024. The register dates every exit, so a gap in the accounts is told apart from a firm that has left.

Throughout the talk, an absent statement means the firm’s accounts are missing from public view. Absence alone tells us neither whether the firm failed to submit nor whether it chose to withhold. The timing and motive for such a decision remain unknown.

The comparison is the RFSD authors’ own. They queried Orbis in April 2023 for Russian entities with a known global ultimate owner and more than $1 million in revenue in 2021, excluding public authorities.

Of the firms with a 2021 statement in the RFSD, 182,641 also appear in that Orbis sample and account for $2.144 trillion in revenue. The 58,835 firms missing from the Orbis sample account for $802 billion in sales, about 27% of RFSD sales in this comparison.

D2a · Data

These four rows compare the dissertation with related work. Each row gives the earlier finding. On the second key press, it shows what the register and the research design let us ask alongside it. The comparison makes no claim of priority.

The RFSD’s authors built the database and reported the first results on filing. In their model pooled over 2012 to 2023, strategic firms file less, by 23 percentage points, and being under sanctions is not directly associated with non-filing. The estimates here are made year by year and in two periods. They agree with the authors for the earlier years and show the decline that followed 2021.

Egorov, Korovkin, Makarin, and Nigmatulina offer the closest firm-level evidence on 2022. They combine customs records with firm balance sheets and find that firms that had imported varieties later sanctioned saw an average 11.9% decline in sales after the invasion, similar in every year through 2024. Their abstract also reports no offsetting expansion by competitors or entrants. That finding is closely related to the replacement result in Chapter 3. For the same years, I study whose accounts remain public and compare firms by ownership and by their own resources. The registry lets me keep firms without statements in view.

The Orbis row is the RFSD authors’ own comparison. Their Orbis sample misses 58,835 firms that have a 2021 statement in the RFSD, with about 27% of the sales in the comparison.

Itskhoki and Ribakova assess the sanctions on the whole economy and describe the impact as mixed, with only moderate contraction reported by official Russian statistics. Firm-level accounts show who contracted, who gained, and who left public view.

Data quality · The RFSD authors’ validationWhy statements, when studies of sanctions turn to satellites

A night-lights product overstates an oil region about ninefold. Statements do not rely on light.

The authors trace part of the error to gas flares at oil wells, which the product does not filter out, and part to output placed in uninhabited areas.

In the dissertation: Section 1.4.3
OpeningSettingFrameworkDataChapter 2Chapter 3What follows37 / 85

D2b · Data

How reliable are Russian firms’ financial statements? The RFSD’s authors report three kinds of checks. The one shown here compares regional totals with official figures.

After 2022 official macroeconomic series were withheld, and studies of sanctions turned to satellite proxies, most often night lights on a grid of one kilometre. The authors compare two gridded products with Rosstat’s official gross regional product for 2015. The product based on night lights reports $37 billion for Moscow against an official $223 billion, and $474 billion for the oil-producing region of Khanty-Mansia against an official $52 billion. They trace part of the upward error to gas flares, which burn gas released during oil extraction and show up as light, and part to the mechanical placement of output in uninhabited areas. Summed statements do not use light, so they avoid this source of error. In the authors’ regressions of each source on official regional product, the RFSD has the highest share of variance explained.

Inside each statement, the authors check that totals equal the sum of their parts, with the tax service’s own equations and its threshold of 4,000 rubles. About 5% of statements do not pass. Their manual review flags 436 firms with 1,130 anomalous statements. A flagged statement still counts as available here, and no amount from it enters a financial measure.

The authors identify a financial incentive to keep industry codes current. Each year a firm confirms its main activity to the Social Insurance Fund. The resulting risk class sets its insurance premium, and state support has also depended on the code. These incentives matter for Chapter 3, which compares firms within four-digit industries.

On the amounts themselves the authors are more guarded. They note evidence that Russian firms, especially non-public ones, manipulate statements, and that later studies show a downward trend.

D4 · Data

Each measurement rule determines which comparisons we can make.

Rosstat supplied statements for 2012 to 2018 and the Federal Tax Service supplied them from 2019. The two providers record zeros differently. I estimate the models separately for 2013 to 2018 and 2019 to 2024, so every year-to-year comparison uses one provider. I compare the 2014 and 2022 episodes across the two sets of estimates.

The release holds no filed statements for 2011. Statements for 2025 are filed on revised official forms, so 2025 is reported as an extension and carries an asterisk throughout.

A filed statement that the RFSD flags as anomalous counts as available, and its amounts are kept out of every financial measure and asset rank. That limits the influence of anomalous values. A missing line is never treated as a zero.

Chapter 3 sets each comparison for 2021 to 2024 against the same comparison for 2015 to 2018.

The slide on the sanctions list shows the two periods side by side. Each has its own model, and every estimated change stays on one side of the switch in 2019.

The five lists are the sanctions list, the government’s list of strategic firms, the president’s list of strategic firms, the 2020 filing-exemption list, and the decree list. Each is matched to the RFSD separately by taxpayer identifier, and a firm can appear on more than one.

Among firms eligible in 2021, 2,977 are on the sanctions list and no other, 426 are on the government’s strategic list and no other, and 3,352,970 are on none. The comparison group is always the firms matched to none of the five.

The lists carry no verified dates, so membership is held fixed across years. That allows a comparison of the same firms before and after 2022. It rules out a comparison around the date a firm was designated.

Two of these lists return when I test the opacity index’s predictions. The sanctions list stands in for enforcement pressure and the 2020 filing-exemption list for the entitlement to withhold.

In the dissertation: Section 2.4, Section 3.4, Section 3.4.4

D7 · Data

Here are the models I’ll use to present the results. Each later slide names its model at the bottom.

Chapter 2 has one model. The outcome is whether a statement is available, yes or no, so the model is a logit. The opacity index with a logistic component gives exactly this form. It is estimated by maximum likelihood, separately for 2013 to 2018 and 2019 to 2024.

Chapter 3 models real revenue by Poisson pseudo-maximum likelihood with firm effects. It fits revenue in levels, keeps recorded zeros, and allows the variance of revenue to differ across firms. Because it fits levels, firms with large sales carry more weight, so each revenue result is also given by least squares on symmetric revenue growth, where each firm counts once. Operating margins are modeled by least squares on the change in the margin.

The replacement test is a regression across 572 four-digit industries, weighted by opening revenue. Its slope is the gain at other firms in rubles for each ruble lost by firms with foreign or joint ownership.

The last row addresses the question from Chapter 2. Outcomes are missing for firms without a statement. I estimate each firm’s probability of being observed using a logit and, separately, CatBoost. I weight observed firms by the inverse of that probability. The scenarios assign sales to firms whose outcomes are missing.

Every estimate in the talk is a conditional association. Standard errors are clustered two ways, by industry and by region, except where a slide says otherwise.

Terms in this part

Availability share
The share of a group’s eligible firms with a statement available in a year.
Transition
One firm’s pair of consecutive years. It ends with a statement available, with none, or with removal from the register.
Odds ratio
The odds of availability, p/(1 − p), for one group divided by the odds for another in the same year, industry, region, legal form, and ownership, and of the same age. One means equal odds.
Predicted probability
The logit’s probability of an available statement, averaged over the sample with every firm set to one list status and then to the other. Gaps are in percentage points.

Firms are ranked each year by their total assets in the preceding year. Of those with a statement for 2021, 95.1% in the highest asset quintile and 83.9% in the lowest also had an available statement in 2022.

With age, year, industry, region, legal form, and ownership held constant, the odds of an available statement in the highest quintile were 3.84 times those in the lowest in 2022. In the opacity index, assets stand in for the counterparty business at stake. Smaller firms have less business that depends on counterparties being able to verify their accounts. They are also the firms most likely to be winding down, and the comparison cannot separate the two.

Chapter 2 · The modelThe one model behind every estimate in this chapter

Every estimate in Chapter 2 comes from one logit for whether a statement is available.

An odds ratio compares two groups at the same values of the other terms. For scale, the slides also give predicted probabilities.

E6a · Chapter 2. Opacity

The last slide showed raw shares. From here the chapter’s numbers are estimates, and they all come from this one model.

On the left is the probability that a firm’s statement is available for a given year. On the right, year effects account for changes common to all firms. The model also includes industry and region effects, along with the firm’s registered legal form, ownership, and age. The last term depends on which comparison we’re making.

There are four comparisons. For size, firms are ranked by assets on the preceding year’s statement. For financial strength, the model adds the operating margin and cash share in the common sample. The other two comparisons are between firms on just one list and firms on no list. The first compares them year by year. The second distinguishes firms that had a statement the year before from those that did not.

An odds ratio compares two groups at the same values of the other terms. For a sense of how common an available statement is, each slide also gives a raw share or an average predicted probability.

Observations in a category whose firms all have a statement, or all lack one, carry no information and are dropped. They never exceed 0.6% of a sample.

E7 · Chapter 2. Opacity

The association between size and statement availability strengthened modestly after 2021. Relative to the lowest asset quintile, the odds ratio for the highest quintile was 13.1% higher in 2022 than in 2021, with a 95% confidence interval from 6.1% to 20.4%. It was 9.2% higher on average in 2023 to 2024. For the fourth quintile, the corresponding increases were 8.2% and 6.2%. The second and third quintiles show no significant change.

The benchmark is 2020, before the invasion, when the same odds ratio was 5.5% lower than in 2021, a difference that was not statistically significant at the 5% level.

All four increases remain positive when an influential industry or region is dropped. Without wholesale trade the later increase for the highest quintile is 5.4% and is no longer statistically significant.

Chapter 2 · Financial positionPrediction 3, with profitability and liquidity added

Assets, operating margin, and cash share each predict continued availability.

Entered together on the same 7,326,679 transitions, each goes with higher odds that a firm’s statement remains available the next year.

ModelThe logit of Equation 2.3, by financial strength · common sample · 95% intervals, clustered by industry and regionIn the dissertation: Section 2.5.5, Table 2.4
OpeningSettingFrameworkDataChapter 2Chapter 3What follows52 / 85

E8 · Chapter 2. Opacity

All three measures come from the preceding year’s statement. They are total assets, the operating margin, and the cash share. The operating margin is profit from sales divided by revenue. The cash share is cash divided by total assets.

The common sample includes 7,326,679 transitions from 2,138,402 firms that reported all three measures the year before. All three measures enter one logit alongside age, year, industry, region, legal form, and ownership.

A firm with twice the assets has 12.9% higher odds of an available statement the next year. A ten-point higher operating margin goes with 2.5% higher odds, and a ten-point higher cash share with 7.1% higher odds. At a base probability of 94.3%, those differences are about 0.6, 0.1, and 0.4 percentage points, respectively. All three are statistically significant at the 1% level.

The year, industry, and region effects absorb what is common to a year, an industry, or a region. The coefficients use what remains, the differences across firms within those cells. They are conditional associations.

Cash has a weaker association with availability when it is the only financial predictor. Its coefficient is 0.156, with a p-value of 0.070. Once size and profitability are held constant, more liquid firms are more likely to have an available statement.

E9 · Chapter 2. Opacity

The opacity index predicts that firms entitled to withhold their accounts will be less visible. Two lists help us examine that prediction.

The 2020 filing-exemption list is the direct counterpart. It covers 22 eligible firms, and none has an available statement for any year from 2019 to 2023. One of the 21 still eligible has one for 2024. The decree exempted these firms from submitting the public copy of their accounts until its repeal at the start of 2023, so their absence while it was in force is what the exemption provides for.

The government’s list of strategic firms identifies a third group, which the state may shield. The RFSD’s authors reported the pattern first. In their linear probability model, strategic status lowers the probability of filing by 23 percentage points in a specification that conditions on the preceding year’s filing. The estimate here confirms it across the eligible population. In 2024 the odds of availability were 97.2% lower than for comparable firms on no list.

The gap covers statements for years before 2022 as well as after, and the archive does not show when those statements left public view.

In the setting section we saw the article’s counts for the lists as issued. Those counts are larger. The 22 and the 426 here count the firms the dissertation matches to the register.

Firms on the sanctions list were more visible than comparable firms before 2019 and less visible by 2024.

In the Rosstat years their odds of a statement were up to 4.55 times those of firms on no list. By 2024 the ratio was 0.57, and the predicted probability 12.6 points lower.

E10 · Chapter 2. Opacity

The first prediction of the opacity index is that firms under more enforcement pressure would be less visible. Here, membership on the sanctions list stands in for that pressure. The first key press shows the Rosstat years and the second shows the years the tax service supplies.

Each point compares two groups of eligible firms. One group consists of firms matched only to the sanctions list. The comparison group consists of firms matched to none of the five lists. The comparison holds age, industry, region, legal form, and ownership constant. The bars give 95% confidence intervals for individual estimates, with standard errors clustered by industry and region. Separate models cover the Rosstat and FNS years.

In 2013 the odds of an available statement were 2.88 times those of firms on no list, and 4.55 times in 2018. In the FNS years the ratio is 1.47 in 2019, 0.95 in 2021, and 0.57 in 2024, when the odds were 43.0% lower than for firms on no list, with an interval from 10.3% to 63.7% lower.

The lists carry no verified dates, so membership is held fixed. Each year therefore compares largely the same firms, and the change from 2021 is estimated more precisely than the levels. By 2024 the odds ratio was 40.1% lower than in 2021, with an interval from 30.9% to 48.2%. The cost is that no comparison can be made around a designation date.

Two details matter here. The change of provider affects the 2019 value. Also, a firm had to exist on its designation date to appear on the list. That can help explain why listed firms were more likely to have an available statement in earlier years.

Each panel comes from its own model. As the measurement slide explained, we can put the two periods side by side, but neither model estimates a change across the 2019 break.

E11 · Chapter 2. Opacity

Each point is the odds ratio for a year relative to its value in 2021. By 2024 it stands at 0.599, which is 40.1% lower than in 2021, with a 95% confidence interval from 30.9% to 48.2%. For 2022 alone the change is 7.5%, with an interval that includes zero.

Among firms still registered at year-end, the 2024 odds ratio is 31.3% lower than in 2021, with an interval from 20.3% to 40.9%. Registry exits alone cannot explain the decline.

In probabilities, the gap between firms on the sanctions list and comparable firms on no list widened from 1.1 percentage points for 2021 to 12.6 for 2024.

One thing changes how the fall is read. The ratio was already falling before the invasion, from 1.47 in 2019 to 1.09 in 2020 and 0.95 in 2021, and the 2019 value is affected by the change of provider. The first year after the invasion contributed little, and most of the decline came in 2023 and 2024.

The model is static. It predicts which firms are opaque and does not date when they became so. An absent statement dates neither a decision nor its motive.

Chapter 2 · Keeping and regaining a statementPrediction 1, split by last year’s statement

Sanctioned firms with a statement kept it. Those without one rarely regained it.

Both states were more persistent for firms on the sanctions list. The 2022 access procedure is one explanation, consistent with the evidence and not identified by it.

ModelThe logit of Equation 2.3, lists by preceding-year statement · firms eligible and registered at both year-ends · 2019 to 2024In the dissertation: Section 2.6.2, Section 2.6.3, Table 2.5
OpeningSettingFrameworkDataChapter 2Chapter 3What follows56 / 85

E12 · Chapter 2. Opacity

Sanctioned firms did not withdraw uniformly. Among firms that had a statement the year before, those on the sanctions list were more likely than comparable firms to keep it, with an odds ratio of 1.73. Sanctioned firms without one were far less likely than comparable firms to regain it, with an odds ratio of 0.17.

The histories of individual firms show the same split. Consider sanctioned firms that were eligible and registered at the end of 2019. Of those firms, 3.52% had a statement in each of 2019, 2020, and 2021, stayed registered, and had no statement in 2022, 2023, or 2024. The corresponding share among firms on no list was 1.31%.

The procedure of 2022 offers one mechanism. A firm could ask the tax service to close public access to all of its statements from 2019 onward. If sanctioned firms used the procedure more often than others, a return would be unlikely, and the firms whose statements stay public would be those with a reason to stay visible, such as customers that require public accounts. The comparisons show both. The RFSD records neither applications nor the dates on which access changed.

This is the cost side of the opacity index at work, as far as the comparisons can show it. A listed firm that still publishes is a firm with a reason to stay visible.

The bar shows Figure 1.4 on one scale. It begins with the 3,357,109 firms eligible in 2021 and shows how many leave at each step in forming the Chapter 3 samples.

The largest group to leave is the 1,226,797 firms with no statement for 2021. That is an outcome Chapter 2 has just modeled, so the selection into Chapter 3 is measured and not assumed. Membership is fixed in 2021. A firm that later stops reporting or leaves the register remains a member, and what happens to it is again an outcome of Chapter 2.

On the predictions slide we left the last column empty. We can now fill in the three Chapter 2 rows.

Each row pairs one of the three predictions from the slide on the opacity index with its finding.

Pressure. Firms on the sanctions list alone were more visible than comparable firms on no list before 2019. In the years the tax service supplies, the odds ratio fell in every year, from 1.47 in 2019 to 0.95 in 2021 and 0.57 in 2024, and by 2024 their predicted probability of an available statement was 12.6 percentage points lower. Entitlement. None of the 22 eligible firms on the 2020 filing-exemption list has a statement for any year from 2019 to 2023. Firms entitled to withhold their accounts withheld them. Firms on the government’s list of strategic firms, which the state may shield, are rarely visible in any year.

Business at stake. Of firms with a statement for 2021, 95.1% of those in the highest asset quintile had one for 2022, against 83.9% of those in the lowest.

All three comparisons go in the direction the index predicts. As we saw on the slide about the register, the date of any decision to withhold and the firm’s reason for it remain unknown.

The available accounts therefore describe larger, financially stronger firms. Chapter 3 follows those accounts. The connection to this chapter will matter again when we see that half of a recorded sales decline comes from sales that left the archive.

Part five · Chapter 3

Adaptation

How did the firms that stay visible adjust?

Terms in this part

Cash sample, inventory sample
Eligible nonfinancial firms whose 2021 statement reports positive sales, positive assets, and cash, or inventories for the inventory sample. Membership is fixed in 2021 and sets no condition on later reporting.
Cash share, inventory share
Cash and equivalents, or inventories, divided by total assets on the same statement.
Symmetric revenue growth
The change in a firm’s real sales divided by its average real sales at the two dates, times 100, in points. A fall from positive sales to zero is −200 points.
Replacement slope
Other firms’ predicted gain in rubles for each additional ruble lost by firms with foreign or joint ownership in the same industry. One is full replacement and zero is none.

Chapter 3 · DesignThe second question: how did the visible firms adjust?

Each comparison after 2021 is set against the same comparison for 2015 to 2018.

The comparisons sort firms on characteristics measured before the war. They describe differences in outcomes and do not identify the effect of holding more cash or inventories.

In the dissertation: Section 3.4, Table 3.2 · * 2025 is on revised forms and is an extension (Sections 1.4.4, 2.2.1).
OpeningSettingFrameworkDataChapter 2Chapter 3What follows61 / 85

F1 · Chapter 3. Adaptation

Chapter 2 ended by identifying the firms we can follow. This chapter follows those firms using the models we saw on the methods slide.

Chapter 3 follows real revenue and operating margins from 2021 through 2024. For revenue, Poisson pseudo-maximum likelihood estimates the conditional mean in levels, includes recorded zeros, and allows the variance to differ across firms. For margins, the model uses ordinary least squares. Standard errors are clustered two ways, by two-digit industry and by region.

Every comparison has a counterpart in the earlier archive. For ownership and for industries the baseline is 2015 to 2018. For cash and inventories the references are shares measured in 2019 and 2020. The contrast shows whether an association belongs to the years after the invasion.

Sorting firms on characteristics measured before the war fixes the groups before firms could respond to the war. The estimates are conditional associations. They also reflect shocks, including the pandemic, that affected firms differently depending on their resources.

Revenue is deflated by the GDP deflator. A common deflator cannot separate a firm’s price changes from changes in the quantity or composition of its sales.

The ownership sample named on the slide is the 1,540,914 eligible nonfinancial firms whose 2021 statement reports positive sales, with positive assets and a known age.

The chapter follows the order of the research question. We look first at how firms adjusted, then examine their own resources, and finish with the replacement test that answers the question about import substitution.

Symmetric real revenue growth is the change in a firm’s real sales divided by its average sales at the two dates, expressed in points. The comparison is with privately owned firms in the same two-digit industry and region, holding assets and age constant. Each firm has equal weight.

Firms with foreign or joint ownership grew faster in all six comparisons within 2015 to 2018, by 13.18 points over the three years. After 2021 the sign reverses. They grew 6.53 points slower over 2021 to 2022 and 3.65 points slower over 2021 to 2024 among firms with positive sales at both dates. With sales that fell to zero counted, the three-year shortfall is 8.01 points, so more than half of it comes from firms whose recorded sales fell to zero.

The shortfall persists in comparisons ending in 2025. It was 5.36 points over 2022 to 2025.

The revenue-weighted estimate is larger, 18.61% lower over 2021 to 2024, and five firms account for 32.9% of its squared influence.

Of the 45,966 firms with foreign or joint ownership in 2021, 9,266, or 20.2%, reported private ownership in 2024. They had held 25.9% of the group’s 2021 sales. In the 2015 cohort the share was 8.7%.

These firms retained most of their sales. In 2024 their real sales were 97.3% of the 2021 level, compared with 77.2% among firms still recorded under foreign or joint ownership.

A change of ownership in the register can reflect different events. Of the 25 largest changes, 15 were re-registrations of Russian businesses held through foreign companies, seven were sales or exits, and three are unclear.

The accounts point to an adjustment that preserved existing businesses. Who acquired those businesses, and on what terms? The accounts leave that distributional question open.

The next slide asks how the firms that left public view fared. After it the chapter turns to a firm’s own resources.

Chapter 2 asked which firms leave public view. This slide asks how those firms fared, from the one source that can say.

Some firms that present no statement for a year report that year’s sales later, in the prior-year column of a later statement. Those recovered sales show how the missing firms fared.

Among firms in the cash sample, real sales fell by a median of 31.0% from 2021 to 2024 when the firm’s 2024 sales appeared only in its 2025 statement, compared with 10.1% when they appeared in the statement for 2024. The gap appears in every year and it widens. Recorded zeros are also more common among the recovered firms, 14.7% against 5.2% for 2024.

The firms whose sales we can recover are a small share of those without a statement, 2.5% for 2024. Their sales suggest how selection affects the comparison.

Firms that leave public view appear to have fared worse than those we can still observe. Comparisons among firms that continue to report therefore probably understate the decline.

That completes the comparison of how firms adjusted. The next slides return to the two resources firms held before the war, the same two identified in the adaptation model.

F8a · Chapter 3. Adaptation

Recall the two resources on the adaptation boundary slide. In the model, inventories sustain sales while a firm seeks another supplier, so their advantage should come first and then fade. Cash helps pay the sunk cost of reorganizing, so its advantage should appear in the second and third years.

Here is what happened to each. A ten-percentage-point higher inventory share in 2021 went with 0.95% higher real revenue in 2022, little difference in 2023, and 0.76% lower revenue in 2024, each relative to 2021. The first-year difference exceeds the average of the next two by 1.38%, with a 95% confidence interval from 0.85% to 1.91%. Half of the firms in the inventory comparison that kept up both sales and margins in 2022 did so with lower real inventories.

One limit matters here. The first-year inventory advantage seen in 2021 also appears in an earlier period. For inventories measured in 2019 it is 1.00%, and for 2020 it is 0.26% with an interval that includes zero.

The accounts show no later gain for firms with higher cash shares. For cash measured in 2021, the average estimate for 2023 and 2024 is −2.08%, with an interval from −3.32% to −0.82%. The negative association is concentrated among firms with foreign or joint ownership, whose sales fell after 2021. Without them the estimate is −0.20%, with an interval from −0.90% to +0.50%. Neither measure of revenue performance shows the predicted gain.

The comparisons sort firms on shares measured before the war. They do not identify the effect of holding more cash or inventories. The slides that follow in the full run give the detail behind each row. After them the chapter ends on the replacement test.

F9 · Chapter 3. Adaptation

With 2021 revenue as the baseline, a ten-percentage-point higher inventory share that year was associated with 0.95% higher real revenue in 2022, 0.08% lower in 2023, and 0.76% lower in 2024. The first-year advantage over the later average is 1.38%, with a 95% confidence interval from 0.85% to 1.91%.

The earlier reference years are the benchmark. For shares measured in 2019 the same contrast is 1.00%, and for 2020 it is 0.26% with an interval that includes zero. A first-year advantage therefore also appears from 2019, and it is largest from 2021.

One caution on measurement. A new accounting standard for inventories applied to statements from 2021, so comparisons of 2021 inventory shares with earlier reference years span a change in accounting rules.

This is the one place the talk uses a causal verb, with its qualifier. Inventories may have cushioned the first year. The design compares firms with different inventory shares before the war. It shows how their subsequent sales differed, while the effect of holding more inventory remains unknown.

The adaptation boundary suggests that cash helps a firm pay the sunk cost of reorganizing, so firms with a higher cash share should retain more sales. The observed association went the other way. A ten-point higher cash share in 2021 went with 2.08% lower real revenue on average in 2023 to 2024.

The estimator explains the sign. Poisson pseudo-maximum likelihood keeps recorded zeros and fits revenue in levels, which the question needs. The cost is that large firms carry the estimate. The 100 most influential firms hold 89.7% of the squared influence on the cash and revenue estimate, against 2.4% for margins, and Figure C.1 reports it.

With ownership and legal form held constant the estimate is −1.64%. Without firms with foreign or joint ownership it is −0.20%, with an interval from −0.90% to +0.50%. The negative association is concentrated among firms with foreign or joint ownership, whose sales fell after 2021.

Margins show no such concentration. A higher cash share predicted a less favorable margin in all twelve comparisons.

F13 · Chapter 3. Adaptation

By 2024 sales are unknown for 15.5% of the cash sample. Inverse probability weights give more weight to observed firms that resemble the missing ones. The weighted estimate applies to all registered members if outcomes are missing at random given the 2021 characteristics, the reporting model is correctly specified, and every member has a positive probability of being observed.

We use two reporting models. For firms with zero cash, their predictions differ. The logit overpredicts their reporting by 9.9, 16.7, and 16.8 percentage points in the three years. Gradient boosting with five-fold cross-fitting keeps the error below 0.06 points and has the lower log loss in all fifteen comparisons. The cash estimate is −2.08% without weights, −1.99% with weights from the logit, and −2.29% with weights from gradient boosting.

A sensitivity analysis then relaxes missing at random. Shifting the missing outcomes by a common factor moves the estimate between −2.35% and −1.72%. Only a shift that grows with the cash share itself, by 18.6% per ten points, turns it positive, to +1.60%.

Chapter 3 · The replacement testLast, the test the opening set up, written as a regression

The replacement slope is other firms’ gain per ruble lost at firms with foreign or joint ownership.

Import substitution predicts a slope near one. A slope of zero means the industries with larger losses saw no larger gains.

F4a · Chapter 3. Adaptation

We’ve seen how firms adjusted and how their outcomes varied with their own resources. The chapter ends with the question about import substitution. In the opening section we saw full replacement as a dashed line. Here is the test behind that line.

The regression uses revenue totals for each four-digit industry. On the right is the loss at firms with foreign or joint ownership, as a share of the industry’s opening revenue. On the left is the change in all other firms’ revenue, divided by the same total. Two-digit industry effects compare industries within a broad sector. The regression also holds constant the share of opening revenue earned by the other firms.

The slope is the predicted change in other firms’ combined sales when the loss is one ruble larger. One is full replacement at the margin and zero is none.

Two cautions matter here. The slope measures whether industries with larger losses also saw larger gains at their other firms. Demand shifts, changes in reporting, and transactions among related firms can affect both quantities. Missing end-year statements also matter for the comparison, so the chapter reports three ways of treating those firms.

The next slide shows the industries, and the one after it the three treatments.

F6 · Chapter 3. Adaptation

What should count as a sales loss when a firm has no end-year statement? The chapter estimates the slope three ways.

Counting a missing end-year statement as a full loss gives a slope of −0.23, with a 95% confidence interval from −0.64 to +0.18. At the upper limit of that interval, other firms gain 0.18 rubles for each additional ruble lost. Omitting still-registered firms without a statement gives −0.34, with an interval from −1.01 to +0.34. Both intervals exclude one, so full replacement is rejected at the 5% level, and neither excludes zero.

The third treatment uses only observed declines and dissolutions. The slope is +0.09. Its interval includes both zero and one, so this comparison cannot distinguish no replacement from full replacement.

Over 2015 to 2018 the loss was 2.6% of the group’s opening sales, against 34.7% after 2021, and the same three slopes are −0.44, −0.21, and +0.41. With 661 industry groups in place of the 572 classes the first slope is −0.20.

Privately owned firms gained no more where the foreign share had been larger.

For ten more points of foreign share in their industry, their revenue grew 0.11 points faster and their operating margin was 0.024 percentage points higher. Neither differs from zero.

F7 · Chapter 3. Adaptation

The protection-rents argument gives two predictions about import substitution. Private incumbents should gain sales where firms with foreign or joint ownership previously held larger market shares. Where those sales carry rents, incumbents’ operating margins should rise.

Among 1,071,648 privately owned firms, ten more points of industry foreign share in 2021 predicted 0.11 points more revenue growth through 2024, with a 95% confidence interval from −0.81 to +1.03, and 0.024 percentage points more operating margin. None of the twelve annual differences is statistically significant. Founding rates in 2024 were no higher in industries with a larger foreign share.

The coefficient describes a conditional association across industries. The broad industry fixed effect absorbs any gain common to firms in that industry. A few large firms can account for substantial sales gains with little change in the average association across firms.
