F14 · Chapter 3. Adaptation

The remaining three rows of the scorecard summarize this chapter. Two predictions lack support.

On the adaptation boundary slide, cash was a means of paying the sunk cost of reorganizing. In the accounts, firms with higher cash shares showed no stronger later performance. The estimate is −2.08%. The negative association is concentrated among firms with foreign or joint ownership. Without them the estimate is −0.20%.

Inventories. A higher inventory share went with 0.95% more revenue in the first year and 0.76% less by the third, which is the timing the model predicts. A first-year advantage of this kind also appears for inventories measured in 2019.

Import substitution. Across 572 industries a larger loss predicted no additional gain at other firms. The slope is −0.23, full replacement is rejected at the 5% level, and the typical private incumbent gained no more where the foreign share of its industry had been larger.

The first findings of the chapter are descriptive and sit outside the scorecard. Recorded sales at firms with foreign or joint ownership fell by 34.7%. About half of that decline comes from the 2021 sales of firms that stayed registered but had no 2024 statement. A quarter of the group’s 2021 sales belonged to firms recorded as privately owned by 2024. Those firms retained 97.3% of their sales.

G1 · What the accounts say, and what follows

Here is the picture from the opening, now with the estimated slope. The band shows its 95% confidence interval.

What do the accounts say about import substitution versus scarring? In the public accounts through 2024, sales contracted at firms with foreign or joint ownership. Domestic competitors in the same industries showed no matching gain, and the accounts show no evidence of rents for the typical private incumbent. Sales at all other firms rose by 5.5% between 2021 and 2024, compared with 2.7% over 2015 to 2018. But they rose no more in the industries where firms with foreign or joint ownership lost more. Those are precisely the industries where import substitution predicts expansion.

The adjustment the accounts point to preserved existing businesses. It ran through inventories and through changes of recorded ownership, some of them sales to domestic owners.

Which firms can be observed is itself selective, in the direction the opacity index predicts.

The answer, row by rowThe whole scorecard

Four predictions match the accounts. The cash prediction and import substitution do not.

Whether the lost sales become hysteresis depends on what follows the restrictions, which lies beyond the 2024 accounts.

G1a · What the accounts say, and what follows

Here is the table from the framework section. We now have a finding for each prediction.

The three rows of the opacity index run in the predicted direction. Firms under more pressure, firms entitled to withhold, and firms with less business at stake are less visible. Public statements as a whole did not become scarcer.

Of the two resources the adaptation boundary named, inventories behaved as predicted and cash did not. A higher cash share showed no stronger sales or operating-margin performance.

Import substitution is not supported. Across 572 industries the slope is −0.23, with an interval from −0.64 to +0.18, and full replacement is rejected at the 5% level. The typical private incumbent gained no more in sales or operating margin where the foreign share of its industry had been larger.

What the accounts point to is an adjustment that preserved existing businesses. It ran through inventories and through changes of recorded ownership, some of them sales to domestic owners.

Scarring in the full sense means that the loss outlasts the restriction. Whether the lost sales persist as hysteresis depends on what follows the restrictions, beyond what the 2024 accounts can show.

G3 · What the accounts say, and what follows

One limit, stated once. The dissertation shows what happened through 2024, with revenue comparisons ending in 2025 as an extension. Lasting scarring is a loss that outlasts the restriction, and establishing it requires accounts from after the restriction ends.

The accounts already give the direction of the evidence. A larger loss predicted no additional gain at other firms, the firms that left the accounts appear to have fared worse than those that stayed, and existing businesses were preserved through changes of recorded ownership. Whether the lost sales become hysteresis depends on what follows the restrictions.

Hysteresis is the term for a loss that persists after the restriction that caused it has ended. The dissertation uses it for the question that stays open.

G4 · What the accounts say, and what follows

Three contributions, each tied to a figure already shown.

The two annual models of statement availability cover 49.1 million Russian firm-years from 2013 through 2024, including years when a firm’s statement was absent from the public archive. Treating availability as an outcome lets us measure how firms with public accounts differ from other eligible firms.

The second contribution is the panel. A reproducible procedure validates the accounting measures and reconciles each firm’s statements with its registration history. That lets us distinguish a gap in the public accounts from a registry exit and establish the sample for each financial outcome.

The third contribution is the replacement test. Across 572 four-digit industries, the regression asks whether other firms gained more where firms with foreign or joint ownership lost more. The import-substitution and scarring interpretations differ on that question. The same test for 2015 to 2018 gives us an earlier comparison.

The theory connects the contributions. The opacity index predicts which firms withhold their accounts, and the adaptation boundary specifies when it pays a firm to reorganize.

G5 · What the accounts say, and what follows

Gradient boosting combines many small decision trees to predict an outcome, such as whether a firm reports revenue. The appendix uses the CatBoost implementation for that one purpose. The proposed extension would apply it to statement availability.

Figure C.3 shows the reason for the extension. Among firms with zero cash, the logit overpredicts revenue reporting by 9.9 to 16.8 percentage points. Gradient boosting keeps the error below 0.06. That comparison motivates four planned steps.

First, compare gradient boosting with the fixed-effects logit for statement availability. We would assess log loss and calibration using five-fold cross-fitting, as in Appendix C.

Second, model the three year-end outcomes together. A firm can have an available statement, have none, or leave the register. Chapter 2 describes how firms move between these outcomes. One joint model would estimate the probabilities of keeping or regaining an available statement and of removal from the register.

Third, use lagged availability and lagged financial measures as predictors, drawing on the 15.3 million transitions of 2020 to 2024.

Fourth, use four-digit industries in Chapter 2, as we already do in Chapter 3.

These are plans. None is in the current results.
